newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Europe burdened by supply, US shines.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Europe burdened by supply, US shines.

text.p: Single currency woes aside, bonds in core Europe are also plagued by heavy supply. Yet again, the U.S. is the bright spot, analysts said on Wednesday.
Alongside Treasuries, gilts and peripheral European markets like Italy and Sweden were top picks on the supply front, while France and Germany were laggards.
"In terms of supply, the U.S. has a good deal to recommend relative to Europe," said Michael Derks, fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
Treasuries fared better on price as well as supply and demand. The U.S. economy was also near the end of a rate rise cycle, unlike most of Europe where growth has been slack.
Investors should shift out of Europe where a busy auction schedule will add to jitters over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said.

"France and Germany are going to overshoot their deficit targets and that means more supply is going to be required. That's going to be a further weight on the bond market," said Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London.
He said more issuance could weigh on the debt-to-GDP ratio in Germany but the EMU emphasis was mainly on the deficit target.

The 10-year U.S. sector was propped up this week by the Treasury's surprise decision to scrap sales of conventional notes in July and October. It plans to offer new five-year inflation-indexed notes in July instead.
Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said progress in cutting the budget deficit and the success of index-linked bond sales had allowed the government to trim the 10-year offer.
"Supply is really tumbling down in the U.S.," said Jan Loeys, global fixed income strategist at J.P. Morgan in London.
Nonetheless, the short end of the U.S. yield curve was "extremely vulnerable" given expectations of a credit tightening in July.
"The short end will get whacked and the long end is going to follow," said Loeys.
In France and Germany where yields were expected to rise, analysts picked short dated paper as a safe strategy.
French OATs gleaned support from domestic demand through EMU storms in the past weeks, but the long end, with little risk premium built into the price, was particularly risky, analysts said.
Gilts were also good value as a safe haven in Europe with the supply scenario seen less burdensome than initially expected, although investors shunned an auction of stock due 2021 last month.
The British government's Public Sector Borrowing Requirement target was likely to be sliced from initial forecasts of 19.2 billion stg at the July 2 budget.
"I think the PSBR is going to be close to 15 billion (sterling). So you could knock off four billion from the funding requirement," said Owens. He favoured the five- to-10-year sector.
Analysts also saw a good value in Italy where the government seems to have abandoned its strategy of sucking up national savings to get into shape for EMU.
"They are continuously cutting the T-bill issues and investors are moving out along the curve," said Loeys.

Sweden was another gem. There was little in the way of supply for the rest of the year after the National Debt Office on Tuesday cut by half its forecast for public borrowing to between zero and 10 billion crowns.
